sections.text:
Abraham, peace be upon him, is the father of the prophets and the friend of the Most Gracious, and one of the most powerful of the messengers who endured the most severe types of trials for the sake of God.

Abraham was born in the city of Babylon in Iraq, in a society steeped in polytheism and the worship of idols and planets.

His father, Azar, was a carpenter and sculptor who made idols with his own hands and sold them to people to worship them instead of God.

Ibrahim grew up seeing these solid stones that were neither useful nor harmful, and his rational mind refused to worship what was made with hands.

He began the journey of searching for the true God. He looked at the planets, then the moon, then the sun, and when he saw it setting, he realized that the true God does not disappear or die.

He became certain that the Creator of this great universe is the One and Only God, and he began calling on his people in a calm, logical dialogue style.

He first went to the person closest to him, which was his father Azar, and said to him with all politeness: “O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear, does not see, and is of no use to you at all?”

But his father became angry and threatened to stone him if he did not deviate from these words. Abraham responded in peace and promised him that he would ask his Lord for forgiveness.

Abraham moved to call his people and told them about the weakness of their idols, but they stuck to the tradition of their fathers without thinking.

Abraham decided to provide them with practical, indubitable proof of the weakness of these idols, so he waited until they left the temple on their holiday day.

Abraham entered the temple, which was filled with large and small idols, and began to destroy them all with his axe. He left the largest idol in it unharmed, and hung the ax around his neck.

When the people returned and found their gods destroyed, they were shocked and asked angrily: “Who did this to our gods?”

They remembered that the boy Abraham was disgracing her, so they brought him to trial before the people and the mighty King Nimrod.

They asked him: “Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?” He answered them with wise sarcasm: “Rather, the eldest of them did this, so ask them if they can speak.”

Here the people stopped in confusion, and they realized deep down that these stones cannot speak or defend themselves.

But pride and stubbornness prompted them to issue a very harsh ruling: “Burn him and support your gods.”

They gathered great firewood for days, and lit a huge fire, the likes of which had never been seen, to the point where birds were burned if they passed over it because of its extreme heat.

Because they could not approach it, they put Ibrahim in a catapult and threw him into the middle of the raging fire.

At that decisive moment, Ibrahim said with complete certainty: “God is sufficient for me and He is the best disposer of affairs.”

Direct divine intervention came, so God commanded the fire, saying: “O fire, be coolness and peace upon Abraham.”

The burning feature of fire was disabled, and Ibrahim emerged from it safe and sound before the eyes of astonished millions.

Despite this amazing miracle, only a few believed in him, including his nephew Lot and his wife Sarah.

Ibrahim migrated with his religion from Iraq to the Levant and then to Egypt, and there he was presented as a gift by the king of present-day Egypt, Hagar.

Ibrahim married Hagar, and God blessed him with his son, Ishmael, after he reached old age.

God tested him again with a harsh test, which was to take his wife Hagar and his infant Ishmael and leave them in a barren valley with no crops or water in Mecca.

Abraham obeyed the command of his Lord, entrusted them to God, and returned.

The Zamzam well exploded for Hagar and her son, and Mecca became a destination for the tribes.

When Ishmael grew up, the greatest test came when Abraham saw in a dream that he was slaughtering his only son.

When the matter was presented to Ismail, he patiently obeyed, and when they submitted to God’s command, God ransomed him with a great ram from Paradise.

Years later, God commanded him to build the Kaaba in Mecca to be the first house built for people to worship God.

Ismail helped him build, and Abraham prayed to his Lord: “Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed, You are the Hearer, the Knower.”

Then he gave people permission to perform Hajj, so that Muslims from all over the world came to this day in response to Hebron’s call.

The lesson of this great story is that certainty in God and complete surrender to His commands is the path to salvation and victory in this world and the hereafter.
